summary: A draft table of contents for a planned Internet Protocol Handbook, a collection of the main internet-family RFCs and experiment notes. It was meant to replace the old ARPANET protocol documents as the internet protocols took over. Replaced by RFC 774.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 766 proposes a table of contents for an Internet Protocol Handbook. The handbook was planned as a collection of existing RFCs and IENs arranged by protocol level.

subtitle: A draft table of contents for a handbook of Internet protocol documents.

tldr.problem: Internet protocol documents were spread across RFCs and Internet Experiment Notes as the Internet protocol family emerged.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC publishes a draft handbook outline grouped into gateway, host, and application levels, plus appendices.
tldr.outcome: RFC 766 is an informational handbook outline and was obsoleted by RFC 774.

facts.label: Handbook type
facts.value: Collection of existing RFCs and IENs

today: RFC 766 is a draft Internet Protocol Handbook outline and was obsoleted by RFC 774.

sections.title: Why Plan a Handbook
sections.content:
The memo says that work on interconnecting networks had produced a family of protocols documented in Internet Experiment Notes (IENs) and RFCs. It describes the Internet protocol family as ready to replace the old ARPANET protocols.

The Network Information Center was to prepare an Internet Protocol Handbook, primarily by collecting existing RFCs and IENs. RFC 766 publishes the current draft table of contents and invites suggestions for additions.
sections.plainLanguage: Internet protocols were documented in many separate notes and RFCs. This memo proposes gathering those documents into one handbook.

sections.title: Proposed Handbook Sections
sections.content:
The draft outline organizes material into Gateway Level, Host Level, and Application Level. Gateway topics include the Internet Datagram Protocol and gateway monitoring; host topics include UDP, TCP, and multiplexing; application topics include time, name, file transfer, Telnet, and message protocols.

Appendices cover assigned numbers, protocol options, address mappings, document file format standards, and mail header format standards. The RFC presents an outline for a compilation, not new protocol specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The planned handbook groups protocols by their role: gateways, hosts, or applications. Appendices would collect reference material such as assigned numbers and address mappings.

sections.title: Accessing RFCs and IENs
sections.content: The memo says RFCs and IENs were public-access files available from the Network Information Center at SRI-KL via FTP. It gives pathname patterns for each type: <NETINFO>IEN-nnn.TXT for IENs and <NETINFO>RFCnnn.TXT for RFCs, noting that the IEN form includes a hyphen and the RFC form does not.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo explains how readers could retrieve the source documents by FTP. It notes a difference in the filename pattern for IENs and RFCs.
